questions.label: Intent
questions.text: In plain English, what is this exercise for, and what happens in it? (exercise control only)
questions.why: It is the yardstick every later answer is checked against.

questions.label: Participants
questions.text: Who are the participants (role and seniority)?
questions.why: Leaders need decisions, not technical steps.

questions.label: Headcount and Teams
questions.text: How many participants, and how many per team?
questions.why: It drives the team count, roles and timing.

questions.label: Proficiency
questions.text: How experienced are the participants with this kind of situation?
questions.why: It sets how hard the scenario can push and how much help the controllers give.

questions.label: Mandate
questions.text: What are the participants responsible for protecting or achieving, and which actions are open to them?
questions.why: It defines what counts as a good decision in play.

questions.label: Time Slot
questions.text: What is the time slot (date, start, length, breaks)?
questions.why: Every move must fit it.

questions.label: Scope Documents
questions.text: Which documents set the scope (terms of reference, contract, agenda)?
questions.why: They are the source of truth for titles and times.

questions.label: Plain English
questions.text: Is English a second language for most participants?
questions.why: It sets the reading level and the acronym rules.

questions.label: Source Limits
questions.text: Must all sources be public? Are there export-control or classification limits?
questions.why: It limits what the AI may use.

questions.label: Real or Fictional World
questions.text: Real country names, or a fictional world?
questions.why: It changes the whole sensitivity profile.

questions.label: Civilian or Military
questions.text: Civilian or military audience?
questions.why: It sets the vocabulary and the frameworks.

questions.label: Recording and AI Use
questions.text: Is performance data recorded, and is AI used on it?
questions.why: Participants must be told plainly.

questions.label: Complements
questions.text: Which existing exercises or mechanisms must this complement, not replace?
questions.why: It sets the framing and the tone.

questions.label: Objectives
questions.text: What should teams practise? List 3–5 objectives, each starting with a verb.
questions.why: Later injects and decisions reference each objective by its ID.
questions.recommended: Assess under uncertainty; decide who leads; share information; coordinate public messages

questions.label: Success Criteria
questions.text: How will you know each objective is met? One per item, in the same order as the objectives.
questions.why: An objective without a test can't be assessed.

questions.label: Success and Failure
questions.text: What counts as success for the participants overall, and what counts as failure?
questions.why: The review measures against it.

questions.label: Teaching Points
questions.text: What one or two teaching points should teams find for themselves?
questions.why: Teaching points are for facilitators. They never appear as takeaways in participant-facing text.

questions.label: Outputs Fed
questions.text: Which outputs must the exercise feed (report sections, AAR structure)?
questions.why: Every capture item should feed one of them.

questions.label: Framework
questions.text: Which competency or norms framework, if any, should decisions map to?
questions.why: Decisions can be mapped to the framework the sponsor uses.

questions.label: Kind of Training
questions.text: What kind of training is this?
questions.why: It sets how the exercise is evaluated and reported.

questions.label: Rules of Engagement
questions.text: What may the participants do, and not do, during play?
questions.why: It keeps play realistic and stops the exercise turning into something it isn't.

questions.label: Deadline
questions.text: Is there a point by which the participants must act, and what happens if they miss it?
questions.why: A fixed point forces the decision the exercise is built around.

stages.title: Premise, Ground Truth and Escalation Ceiling

questions.label: One-Line Problem
questions.text: One-line problem: what goes wrong, for whom, and what must leaders decide?
questions.why: Everything else is built on it. Offer three options drawn from the objectives.

questions.label: Participant Description
questions.text: In one paragraph a participant could read, what is the scenario about?
questions.why: Catalogs, invitations and read-ins all start from it. It must not give the twist away.

questions.label: Place and Time
questions.text: Where and when is the scenario set: region, era, time of year?
questions.why: Places and dates stay consistent across every inject and document.

questions.label: Obvious Explanation
questions.text: What is the "obvious" explanation, and what is really happening?
questions.why: A plausible innocent cause that is true but not the whole story trains assessment under uncertainty.

questions.label: Ground Truth
questions.text: List the ground-truth facts, one per item: what really happens (exercise control only).
questions.why: Only exercise control knows the ground truth. Later checks use these facts to catch leaks.

questions.label: Threat Actor Type
questions.text: What is the threat actor type?
questions.why: It sets the whole threat story. A non-state actor with no home country blames no state.

questions.label: Threat Actor Capability
questions.text: How capable is the threat actor? (exercise control only)
questions.why: It bounds what the adversary can plausibly do in play.

questions.label: Motive
questions.text: What is the actor's motive?
questions.why: It must not target a government, political system, religion or ethnic group.

questions.label: Way In
questions.text: How does the attacker get in, and how does the attack work (in plain terms)?
questions.why: Keep it simple and common: leaders decide better on an attack they recognise.

questions.label: ATT&CK Techniques
questions.text: Which ATT&CK techniques does the adversary use? One per item, such as "T1566 Phishing" (exercise control only).
questions.why: Techniques tie the scenario to real behaviour, and to the injects and detections that test it.

questions.label: Escalation Ceiling
questions.text: What is the escalation ceiling: the worst it gets, and what never happens?
questions.why: It keeps the exercise inside what teams can discuss in the time.
questions.recommended: Never a full outage, nobody hurt, no data stolen, no state blamed

questions.label: Real and Fictional
questions.text: What is real and what is fictional?
questions.why: Participants must be able to tell the two apart.
questions.recommended: Real: countries, season, holidays (background only). Fictional: every organization, person, event and number

questions.label: Ending
questions.text: How does it end?
questions.why: Teams need a resolution to discuss in the after-action review.
questions.recommended: Cause known and a fix planned, before the exercise's deadline

questions.label: Red Herring
questions.text: Is there a red herring?
questions.why: One per exercise at most, clearly marked in the ground truth.

questions.label: Symmetry
questions.text: Does the incident hit every participating state in the same way?
questions.why: Symmetry keeps any one state from being singled out.

questions.label: Population
questions.text: Who else populates the scenario world (press, public, staff, simulated users), and roughly how many?
questions.why: Injects need voices, and simulated users (NPCs) have to be generated before play.

questions.label: Information Environment
questions.text: Which news, social media, email and chat platforms exist in the scenario world, and who uses them?
questions.why: Information injects need somewhere to appear, and the same platforms every time.

questions.label: Notional Network
questions.text: What networks and systems does the scenario's story describe?
questions.why: Injects and documents describe the same systems every time, and the network module can build them later.

questions.label: Live Range
questions.text: Does any part of the exercise run on a live range or real systems?
questions.why: A live part needs a network built for it; a discussion needs only the story.

stages.title: Events, Decisions and Rules of Play

questions.label: Key Events
questions.text: What events (injects) does exercise control push, in order? One per item: when, who delivers it, what happens, and the response you expect (exercise control only).
questions.why: They make sure every objective gets tested, whatever the participants do.

questions.label: Decision Points
questions.text: Which decisions must the participants make, and when? One per item (exercise control only).
questions.why: They are where the exercise does its teaching.

questions.label: Branching
questions.text: How does the scenario change depending on what the participants do? (exercise control only)
questions.why: Controllers need to know which way to steer before play starts.

questions.label: Escalation Steps
questions.text: What are the escalation steps, in order? One per item; mark the last one the participants can still recover from (exercise control only).
questions.why: Controllers can see how close play is to the ceiling.

questions.label: Pacing
questions.text: How does time run in the exercise?
questions.why: It decides how injects are timed and how long each decision can take.

questions.label: Scenario Clock
questions.text: How does scenario time map to real time, such as "one move is six hours"?
questions.why: Participants and controllers need the same sense of how much time has passed.

questions.label: Adjudication
questions.text: Who decides the outcome of what participants do?
questions.why: Someone has to rule on what each action achieves, and everyone should know who.

questions.label: Fog
questions.text: How much of the picture do participants see?
questions.why: What they are not shown, on purpose, is part of what the exercise tests.
questions.recommended: Partial: each role sees what it would
options: Partial: each role sees what it would
Full: only what is reported to them

stages.title: Names, Vocabulary and the First Sensitivity Review

questions.label: Exercise Name
questions.text: What is the exercise's name?
questions.why: Two words, easy to say aloud in a second language, and not reused from an earlier exercise.

questions.label: Organizations
questions.text: Which organizations appear in the scenario, and whose side is each on: friendly, adversary or neutral? One per item, such as "Harrow Port Authority: friendly".
questions.why: As few names as possible, and each name says what it is ("… Bank", "… Telecom").

questions.label: Threat Actor Name
questions.text: What is the threat actor's name?
questions.why: Check it for meaning in the region's languages, and for links to films, books, games or real groups.

questions.label: National Bodies
questions.text: How are national bodies named?
questions.why: Naming them by role keeps every state equal.
questions.recommended: By role only: "your central bank", "your ministry"

questions.label: Fixed Terms
questions.text: Which words are fixed?
questions.why: The vocabulary list is enforced in every artifact.

questions.label: Banned Terms
questions.text: Which words are banned?
questions.why: The vocabulary list is enforced in every artifact.

questions.label: Public Handles
questions.text: How are members of the public shown?
questions.why: Generated handles avoid real people's names.
